filings.topic: TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control
filings.content:
TCP BBR vs CUBIC Congestion Control

CUBIC is a loss-based congestion control algorithm that increases the congestion window until packet loss occurs, then reduces it — often filling network buffers and adding latency. BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is a model-based algorithm that measures the bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, then paces packets to operate at that point without filling buffers.

Key Differences

  • Approach: CUBIC reacts to loss; BBR builds a model of the network path.
  • Buffer behavior: CUBIC tends to fill buffers (bufferbloat); BBR avoids queue buildup.
  • Latency: BBR typically maintains lower latency on buffer-bloated links.
  • Throughput: CUBIC can achieve higher throughput on short, high-bandwidth paths with shallow buffers.

Practical Implications

BBR is generally preferred for latency-sensitive applications and networks prone to bufferbloat. CUBIC remains the default in many Linux kernels and performs well in data-center environments with well-managed queues.

filings.content:
CAP theorem

The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store under a network partition cannot simultaneously guarantee consistency and availability — it must choose one. During a partition you either go CP (refuse writes to stay consistent) or AP (keep serving requests and reconcile later). When no partition exists, both consistency and availability are achievable, so the real design decision is how the system behaves during failures.

Consistency

Every read receives the most recent write or an error. All nodes see the same data at the same time.

Availability

Every request receives a response (non-error), without guaranteeing it reflects the most recent write.

Partition tolerance

The system continues operating despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed between nodes. Partitions are unavoidable in distributed networks, so partition tolerance is not optional.

Practical trade-off

  • CP: prioritise consistency; reject or block writes during a partition until it heals.
  • AP: prioritise availability; keep accepting reads and writes, then reconcile divergent state after the partition ends.

Many systems are tunable (e.g., quorum reads/writes) and can shift along the CP–AP spectrum depending on configuration and failure conditions.

What is quantization in LLM models?

Quantization is the process of reducing the precision of model weights from 16 or 32 bit down to 8, 4, or even fewer bits. This makes the model significantly smaller and speeds up computation, at the cost of a slight decrease in accuracy.

Why GGUF is faster for local inference

GGUF is a file format designed to store quantized weights with a memory layout that maps efficiently into RAM. Because the data is already in a compact, optimized structure, loading and accessing it during inference is much quicker than with traditional formats. This makes GGUF especially suitable for running large language models locally on consumer hardware.

The combination of quantization and the GGUF format enables faster token generation and lower memory usage without needing high-end server-grade equipment.

filings.topic: TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control
filings.content:
TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control

CUBIC is a loss-based congestion control algorithm: it grows the congestion window until packet loss occurs, then backs off. Because it relies on loss as a signal, it tends to fill router buffers, which increases queuing latency (bufferbloat).

BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is model-based. It continuously measures the bottleneck bandwidth and minimum round-trip time, then paces transmission to operate at the bandwidth-delay product without deliberately filling buffers.

In practice, BBR typically achieves lower latency on buffer-bloated links, while CUBIC can perform better on short, high-bandwidth paths where loss is cheap and buffer occupancy is less of a concern.

  • CUBIC: loss-based, window grows until loss, then multiplicative decrease; higher latency under bufferbloat.
  • BBR: model-based, paces sends at measured bandwidth/RTT operating point; lower latency, less buffer pressure.

ACLs gate which tailnet nodes can reach which ports. A regular ACL rule specifies which sources can reach which destinations and ports, using user identities (e.g., group:admins). Key difference: Regular ACLs use user identities (e.g., group:admins) to control access, while tags replace user identities with role-based node identities (e.g., tag:server), making access persistent across user changes.

filings.content:
CAP Theorem in Distributed Systems

The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties simultaneously: Consistency (all nodes see the same data at the same time), Availability (every request receives a response), and Partition tolerance (the system continues operating despite network partitions).

Since network partitions are inevitable in distributed systems, the practical choice is between CP (sacrifice availability during a partition to maintain consistency) and AP (sacrifice consistency to remain available, reconciling conflicts later). When no partition exists, both consistency and availability can be achieved.

  • CP systems (e.g., traditional RDBMS with synchronous replication, ZooKeeper): refuse writes or return errors during a partition to prevent divergent data.
  • AP systems (e.g., Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak): accept writes on all reachable nodes and resolve conflicts via eventual consistency mechanisms like vector clocks or CRDTs.

The theorem does not mean you must pick one forever; many modern databases offer tunable consistency levels per operation.

clawbot.final_text: Created lesson "Quantization in LLM models" (slug: lesson-324e4fc08ccf) covering quantization definition, how it works, GGUF format benefits, and trade-offs.

filings.content:
What is quantization in LLM models?

Quantization is the process of reducing the precision of neural network weights from 16-bit or 32-bit floating-point numbers to lower bit depths like 8-bit, 4-bit, or even less. This reduction makes the model parameters smaller in memory footprint and enables faster arithmetic operations during inference, at the cost of a slight decrease in model accuracy.

How does quantization work?

Instead of storing full-precision floating-point values that require more memory bandwidth and computational resources, quantized models use integer representations or reduced-precision floating-point formats. For example, a 32-bit float becomes an 8-bit integer, dramatically reducing the amount of data that needs to be loaded from memory and processed by the CPU or GPU.

Why is GGUF faster for local inference?

GGUF (GPT-Generated Format) is a file format specifically designed to store quantized model weights with an optimized memory layout. The format maps quantized weights directly into system memory in a way that minimizes memory access patterns and maximizes cache efficiency. This layout enables faster loading and more efficient computation on local hardware compared to traditional model formats, making GGUF particularly suitable for running large language models on consumer-grade hardware.

What are the trade-offs?

While quantization significantly reduces model size and speeds up inference, it introduces quantization error that can affect the model's output quality. However, modern quantization techniques and fine-tuning methods have minimized this accuracy loss to acceptable levels for most applications, especially when using higher bit depths like 8-bit rather than extreme compression like 2-bit.

filings.content:
Tailscale ACLs Overview

Tailscale ACLs control which devices (nodes) can communicate with each other and on which ports.

Regular ACL Rules

Regular ACL rules specify which sources can reach which destinations and ports. For example: group:admins can reach tag:server on port 22.

Tags vs. User-Based Rules

A tag is an identity assigned to a device itself, rather than to a person. When a device is tagged, it stops being owned by a specific user. This means servers can maintain access to tagged devices even after the original user leaves.

Key difference: regular ACLs are user-centric (you grant access to a person), while tags are node-centric (you grant access to a device identity). Tags provide better access control for dynamic or rotating node identities.

  • Tags persist across user changes
  • ACL rules can reference tags or groups
  • Use tags for infrastructure-level access management

filings.content:
The CAP theorem states that a distributed data store can guarantee at most two of three properties at any given time: Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. Because a network partition is inevitable in distributed systems, the practical choice is between CP (consistency + partition tolerance, refusing writes during a partition) or AP (availability + partition tolerance, serving reads/writes and reconciling later).

Why it matters

During a partition, you cannot simultaneously serve every request and return a consistent value for every replica. Picking CP means some clients get errors; picking AP means they may read stale or conflicting data that must be reconciled after the partition heals.

Common misconceptions

  • CAP is not a binary switch — it describes trade-offs under failure, not a permanent property of the system.
  • When there is no partition, both consistency and availability hold, so the real decision is what to do during failures.
  • Many systems claim "AP" but still prioritize consistency through background reconciliation, which blurs the line.

How to choose

  1. CP: use when correctness matters more than uptime (e.g., financial ledgers, configuration stores).
  2. AP: use when serving users matters more than perfect consistency (e.g., social feeds, caches).

filings.content:
Heartbeat escalation

Each member node sends a heartbeat signal at a regular interval. The hub monitors freshness of these signals in real time. If a member misses N consecutive beats, its state transitions to stale, then degraded. Only after the degraded window passes without recovery does the system escalate to a page alert. This multi-stage design means a single missed beat or a brief wifi flap never triggers a phone page.
